note: A small study atlas, not a complete ancient gazetteer. Marker coordinates are rounded orientation points; no ancient borders, routes or territorial claims are drawn. Connections to syllabus authors/works are editorial study pairings. Mythic entries are kept out of dated historical filtering.

places.title: Athens · Acropolis
places.body: A civic and religious setting for studying Athenian culture. The Parthenon building programme belongs to 447–432 BCE. The location marker represents the Acropolis, not the whole ancient city.
places.people: Socrates, Plato and the Athenian dramatists: reading connections, not claimed birthplaces.

places.title: Delphi · Sanctuary of Apollo
places.body: A sanctuary and oracle with influence across Greek communities. Its historical religious role should be distinguished from stories about divine speech and the mythical centre of the world.
places.event: Growing religious and political influence in the 6th century BCE
places.people: Read beside Herodotus and the account of the oracle in Plato's Apology.

places.title: Troy · Archaeological site
places.dates: Multiple occupation layers; epic events not securely dated
places.body: An archaeological site with many phases of occupation. Its literary association with the Iliad does not make each Homeric episode an excavated historical fact.
places.event: Archaeological layers versus later epic storytelling
places.people: Homeric tradition: study the poems alongside the distinction between material remains and narrative.

places.title: Troy · The epic war
places.dates: Undated here: narrative time is not a verified historical date
places.body: Achilles, Hector and Priam belong to the poem's account of a war at Troy. This marker shares a literary association with the real site; it is not evidence that the characters or narrated actions are historically established.
places.event: The Iliad's conflict and its aftermath in later epic

places.title: Rome · Historic centre
places.body: A layered urban setting for Roman political writing, historical narrative and architecture. Read the city's literary claims against its changing institutions and monuments rather than imagining one unchanging Rome.
places.event: Republican and imperial monuments coexist with later transformations
places.people: Cicero, Virgil and Roman historians: editorial reading connections.

places.title: Pompeii · Vesuvian towns
places.body: The eruption of Vesuvius buried Pompeii and neighbouring settlements in 79 CE. Buildings and objects provide evidence of urban life; the chosen point is a general Pompeii marker, not the full UNESCO multi-site boundary.
places.people: Pair the imperial-history module with material evidence and the existing Roman architecture course.

places.title: Carthage · Punic and Roman city
places.body: Rome destroyed Punic Carthage in 146 BCE; a Roman city later occupied the site. The source's opening description gives BCE correctly, although one later paragraph contains an inconsistent AD label.
places.people: Read beside Roman historical narratives and Augustine; distinguish their different periods.

places.title: Carthage · Dido and Aeneas
places.dates: Undated legendary encounter in the Aeneid
places.body: Virgil's encounter between Dido and Aeneas is a literary story connected with Carthage, not a dated historical meeting. Compare what the poem does with place, belonging and imperial destiny.
places.people: Virgil and the poem's legendary protagonists.
